source: NCERT Class X, Contemporary India II, Geography Ch. 1.

sections.heading: 1. Resources — Meaning and Classification
points: A **resource** = anything in our environment which can be used to satisfy our needs, provided it is **technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable**.

points.text: Resources are classified on the basis of:
sub: **Origin** — biotic (living, e.g. flora, fauna) and abiotic (non-living, e.g. rocks, metals).
**Exhaustibility** — renewable (solar, wind, water, forests) and non-renewable (minerals, fossil fuels).
**Status of development** — potential, developed, stock and reserve.

sections.heading: 2. Development of Resources — and Sustainability
points: Indiscriminate use of resources led to problems: **depletion** for a few, **accumulation** in few hands, and **ecological crises** (global warming, pollution, land degradation).
**Sustainable development** = development without harming the environment and without compromising the needs of future generations.
The **Rio Earth Summit (1992)** and **Agenda 21** promoted global sustainable development and local action.

sections.heading: 3. Resource Planning in India
points: **Resource planning** is essential because resources are unevenly distributed (e.g. Jharkhand/Chhattisgarh have minerals but lack water/infrastructure; Rajasthan has solar/wind but lacks water).
Planning involves identification of resources, planning structure, and matching resources with development plans.
**Conservation of resources** — stressed by leaders like **Gandhiji**: 'There is enough for everybody's need but not for anybody's greed.'

sections.heading: 4. Land Resources and Land Use
points: India's land is used as **forests, land not available for cultivation, other uncultivated land, fallow land and net sown area**.
**Net sown area** is highest in Punjab and Haryana; forest area is below the desired **33%** (per National Forest Policy).
**Land degradation** causes: deforestation, overgrazing, mining, over-irrigation (salinity/waterlogging), industrial effluents.

sections.heading: 5. Soils of India
points: **Alluvial** — most fertile and widespread (northern plains, deltas); rich in potash, ideal for cereals.
**Black (regur)** — from lava (Deccan), retains moisture, ideal for **cotton**.
**Red and Yellow** — on crystalline rocks (Deccan, eastern/southern); reddish due to iron.
**Laterite** — high rain, leaching; good for tea, coffee, cashew.
**Arid** — sandy, saline (Rajasthan); **Forest** — in hilly/mountain areas.
**Soil erosion** by wind/water (gully → badlands e.g. Chambal ravines); prevented by **contour ploughing, terrace farming, shelter belts, strip cropping**.

sections.heading: 6. High-Yield One-Liners (Last-Minute Recall)
points: Resource = technologically accessible + economically feasible + culturally acceptable.
Classification: origin (biotic/abiotic), exhaustibility (renewable/non-renewable), ownership, development.
Rio Earth Summit 1992 → Agenda 21 (sustainable development).
Desired forest cover = 33% (National Forest Policy).
Black soil = cotton (regur, Deccan lava); Alluvial = most fertile, cereals; Laterite = tea/coffee.
Chambal ravines = badlands (gully erosion).

sections.heading: 7. Common Traps (Watch Out)
points: **Black soil (regur)** is best for **cotton**, formed from **lava/basalt** (Deccan).
**Alluvial soil** is the **most fertile and widespread**.
**Agenda 21** came from the **Rio Earth Summit (1992)**.
The desired forest cover for India is **33%** of geographical area.
